figures.shows: Block diagram of the QASA architecture: tokenization of temporal tokens, positional encoding, (n_layer - N) standard Transformer encoder layers (multi-head attention, layer normalization, feed forward network), then N quantum encoder layers in which a VQC block sits beside the attention and feed forward blocks, then a prediction or downstream head.
figures.confirmed_by: The model consists of N −1 standard Transformer encoder layers followed by one Quantum Encoder Layer.

figures.shows: Circuit diagram of the deployed PQC on 8 data qubits plus one ancilla: an encoding column of RX and RZ rotations on each qubit, then three blocks of single-qubit rotations followed by a ring of CNOTs with an ancilla coupling and an RY on the ancilla; Pauli-Z measurement on all data qubits at the end.
figures.confirmed_by: The deployed circuit has 36 trainable angles and 27 CNOTs in total (exact counting convention in Table 3).

figures.shows: Nine small panels (rows: Traditional Transformer, QASA_classical, QASA; columns: epoch 1, 15, 30) of prediction (red) against true signal (blue) on the damped oscillator task. At epoch 1 all three predictions are near flat. At epoch 15 the QASA prediction follows the oscillation while the other two stay near flat. At epoch 30 QASA follows the true signal closely, QASA_classical follows it partly, and the Traditional Transformer follows only the late small oscillations.
figures.confirmed_by: At epoch 30, QASA achieves near-perfect predictions, indicating much faster convergence compared to both the classical and transformer baselines.

figures.shows: Training and validation loss (y, 0 to 1.2) against epoch (x, 0 to 45) for the quantum model (blue) and the classical QASA_classical model (red), train solid and validation dashed. Both stay near 1.0 for the first 15 to 18 epochs, then fall steeply; the red classical curves fall about 2 epochs before the blue quantum curves; both end near 0.02. An embedded table marks minimum validation loss 0.0085 (quantum) and 0.0122 (classical), and minimum training loss 0.0106 (quantum) and 0.0219 (classical).
figures.confirmed_by: The quantum model reaches a lower minimum validation loss (0.0085) than the classical model (0.0122) with smoother convergence.

figures.shows: Two panels on the chaotic logistic task, mean of 3 seeds. (a) Normalised singular value (y, log scale, 1e-4 to 1) against singular value index (x, 1 to 20) for four series: QASA before quantum, QASA after quantum, classical bottleneck after, classical full final layer; all fall by about 3 orders of magnitude; the classical bottleneck lies lowest. (b) Cumulative spectral energy fraction (y, 0.5 to 1.0) against number of components (x, 1 to 20); at one component the classical bottleneck is at about 0.98, QASA after about 0.87, classical full about 0.66, QASA before about 0.51; all reach about 1.0 by about 8 components.
figures.confirmed_by: both bottleneck realisations (QASA and the classical bottleneck) reach near-unity variance in far fewer components than the full classical model.

figures.shows: Chaotic logistic task, seed 42. Top row: PCA projections (PC1 against PC2, points coloured by time step 0 to 19) before the quantum layer (PC1 66.4 percent, PC2 15.9 percent), after the quantum layer (PC1 71.2 percent, PC2 15.7 percent) and from the classical final layer (PC1 62.8 percent, PC2 18.3 percent). Bottom left: cumulative explained variance (y, 0.65 to 1.0) against PCA components (x, 1 to 20). Bottom centre and right: 20 by 20 pairwise cosine similarity heat maps; the QASA after-quantum map is almost uniformly dark red (about 1.0 for all time-step pairs); the classical final-layer map is a checkerboard of values from about -0.25 to 1.0.
figures.confirmed_by: Bottom center/right: pairwise cosine similarity matrices reveal that the quantum layer produces more structured temporal correlations than the classical model.

figures.shows: Seed 42. Left: effective rank (y, 0 to 8) for chaotic logistic, damped oscillator and square wave; before quantum layer about 8.1, 2.3 and 1.9; after quantum layer about 2.6, 1.7 and 1.5; classical about 5.7, 2.4 and 2.0. Right: mean L2 norm of the quantum correction (y, 0 to 9): about 7.7 for chaotic logistic, about 8.9 for damped oscillator, about 8.4 for square wave.
figures.confirmed_by: The quantum layer’s dimensionality reduction is largest on the chaotic logistic task (here ∆ = −5.5 for this seed; −4.1 on the 3-seed average of Table 9)

figures.shows: Mean gradient variance Var(dC/dtheta) (y, log scale, 1e-4 to about 3e-1) against number of qubits (x, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12) with error bars, for QASA 1 layer (red, solid) and QASA 4 layers (blue, dashed), with a dotted barren plateau threshold at 1e-4. The 1-layer series falls from about 0.06 at 4 qubits to about 0.02 at 12 qubits. The 4-layer series falls from about 0.02 at 4 qubits to about 0.0001 at 12 qubits, about on the threshold. The error bars are wide on both series, spanning about an order of magnitude or more, and the lower bars of the 4-layer series reach below the 1e-4 threshold at 8 to 12 qubits.
figures.confirmed_by: QASA’s single-layer design (red) maintains trainable gradients across all qubit counts, while the 4-layer design (blue) exhibits exponential decay characteristic of barren plateaus.

figures.shows: Test MAE (y) against input sequence length L (x, 20, 48, 96) in two panels, 1 seed, 80 epochs, for the full classical Transformer (blue), the classical bottleneck (green) and QASA (red). Chaotic logistic (y about 0.29 to 0.34): classical full about 0.335, 0.336, 0.329; the two bottleneck series both flat at about 0.294. Seasonal trend (y about 0.55 to 1.1): classical full about 0.60, 1.08, 0.84; the two bottleneck series nearly overlap, about 0.77, 0.74, 0.57.
figures.confirmed_by: The two bottleneck models (classical bottleneck, green; QASA, red) track each other near-identically across L

papers.what_it_is: A case study of a hybrid quantum Transformer (QASA) that puts a 36-parameter circuit in the final encoder layer, used to argue that a capacity-matched classical bottleneck explains the gain over a full-capacity classical Transformer.

assertions.value: The authors state that QASA is a hybrid Transformer that replaces the value projection of a single encoder layer with a 36-parameter parameterized quantum circuit, keeping all other layers classical.

figures.shows: Pipeline diagram: a 512-unit ResNet feature vector enters a pre-VQC fully connected layer with GELU, then a 9-qubit amplitude encoding and a strongly entangling PQC (a rotation R(alpha, beta, gamma) on each qubit followed by CNOTs), then Pauli-Z measurements on each qubit, then a 3-class output layer.
figures.confirmed_by: In Figure 1, the proposed quantum machine learning pipeline is depicted.

figures.shows: Six example MRI scans from the test set, each with the true label, predicted class and softmax probabilities. Four are classified correctly (brain_tumor, brain_glioma, brain_glioma, brain_glioma). Two true meningioma scans are misclassified: one as brain_glioma with probabilities about 0.64, 0.35, 0.01 and one as brain_tumor with probabilities about 0.01, 0.24, 0.76.
figures.confirmed_by: Figure 2 presents a qualitative view of the predictions produced by the QML on the given MRI scans from the test set.

figures.shows: RGA score (y, 0 to 1) against fraction of data removed (x, 0 to 1), mean across 5 folds, one line per model (Linear, RF, SVM, MLP, QML). All curves are near 1.0 up to about 0.6 removed. Linear and MLP bend down from about 0.6 to 0.8 removed (about 0.96 at 0.8); RF, SVM and QML stay near 1.0 to about 0.9. All five curves fall steeply to 0.0 at 1.0 removed.
figures.confirmed_by: All models maintain a nearly perfect ranking accuracy when less than 40% of the data are removed.

figures.shows: RGR score (y, about 0.69 to 1.0) against noise standard deviation in percent (x, 0 to 300), mean across 5 folds, per model. Linear falls fastest, to about 0.69 at 300 percent; RF falls to about 0.75. SVM stays near 1.0 to about 120 percent then falls to about 0.83 at 300 percent. MLP and QML begin to fall earlier, track each other, lie above SVM from about 160 to about 280 percent, and end at about 0.82 at 300 percent.
figures.confirmed_by: The QML achieves the highest overall robustness, as reflected by the largest AURGR value, indicating a slower and more controlled degradation under increasing noise.

figures.shows: Two panels of RGR score against attack strength, mean across 5 folds. Top, FGSM feature perturbation (x, epsilon 0 to 0.30; Linear, MLP, QML only): Linear drops to about 0.39 at 0.10 and about 0.30 at 0.30; MLP and QML stay near 1.0 to 0.05, QML above MLP, ending at about 0.38 (QML) and about 0.35 (MLP) at 0.30. Bottom, spatial image perturbation (x, strength 0 to 40; all five models): SVM is highest from about 10 to 30; at strength 40 RF is highest at about 0.845, SVM and MLP about 0.82, Linear about 0.79 and QML lowest at about 0.775.
figures.confirmed_by: Under FGSM perturbations, QML achieves the highest robustness among the evaluated models.

figures.shows: Six versions of one MRI slice at 0, 20, 40, 60, 80 and 100 percent occluded area, with the most Grad-CAM-relevant square patches replaced by a Gaussian-blurred baseline; the image is progressively blurred until it is fully blurred at 100 percent.
figures.confirmed_by: Figure 6 shows an example of an input image under progressive occlusion.

figures.shows: RGE score (y, about 0.5 to 1.0) against occluded image area in percent (x, 0 to 100), mean across 5 folds, per model. All curves fall from 1.0 to about 0.5 at 100 percent. Linear is lowest through about 70 percent (about 0.585 at 50 percent). RF and SVM are highest at about 20 to 40 percent (about 0.88 at 20 percent). QML lies between Linear and the other models at about 30 to 50 percent and close to MLP at about 60 to 100 percent. SVM is non-monotonic near 90 percent.
figures.confirmed_by: Random Forest achieves the highest overall RGE, indicating strong stability of predictions when visual information is systematically removed.

figures.shows: Radar plot with six axes (F1, RGA, AURGA, AURGR, AURGR Spatial, AURGE, plus AURGR FGSM) of min-max normalized metrics per model. SVM (orange) has the largest polygon on F1, RGA, AURGA and AURGR Spatial; QML (purple) is close to SVM on F1, RGA and AURGA, equal to the largest on AURGR and highest on AURGR FGSM, but about 0.4 on AURGR Spatial and AURGE; RF is highest on AURGE; Linear is near 0 on most axes; RF and SVM are set to zero on the FGSM axis for display.
figures.confirmed_by: The QML remains highly competitive, achieving the strongest robustness to Gaussian feature noise and the highest FGSM robustness among the models for which this attack is evaluated
